title: Publish an upgrade note for the 0.8.0 retained-snapshot incompatibility: one newer file makes a whole scope unusable to an older lore
description:
Routed by opum-agent 2026-09-20 as part of the ODOC-231 decomposition, framed as a consequence of the LCLI-546 epic. MEASURED HERE BEFORE FILING, AND THE FRAMING CHANGES: this incompatibility is ALREADY PUBLISHED. It is not a future cost of the epic, and the note is owed now rather than at the epic's release.

WHAT WAS MEASURED, all against this repository:

- The three optional edgeValue keys (statement, version, relationOrdinal) are at src/core/snapshot.ts:179-181, inside a .strict() object, landed by commit dd0876dc "feat(LCLI-540): carry the ADR-0021 relation qualifiers into retained edges (#170)" on 2026-09-18. LCLI-540 is Done.
- `git show v0.8.0:src/core/snapshot.ts | grep -c relationOrdinal` returns 3, so the keys are IN the v0.8.0 tag.
- `npm view @opum-ai/lore dist-tags` returns latest = 0.8.0. So the incompatible writer is the version consumers install by default, today.

BLAST RADIUS, verified in src/core/snapshot-store.ts rather than taken from the routing message. listSnapshots() readdir's the scope directory and calls loadSnapshot() on EVERY entry (line 123); the drain path parses every entry likewise (lines 206-219); and retainSnapshot() calls listSnapshots() first (line 55). parseRetainedSnapshot throws on an unrecognised key because the schema is .strict(). So a single file written by 0.8.0 makes the entire scope throw for list, load, retain AND drain on an older binary -- the failure is scope-wide, not per-file, and it takes out the drain path that a consumer would reach for to clear it.

THE ASYMMETRY IS THE POINT, AND IT IS NOT A BUG. Ruling 13 already handles the forward direction: isRetainedQualifierBackfill (snapshot-store.ts:55-68) stops a NEWER lore reporting an OLDER file as corrupt. The reverse cannot be fixed the same way, because it would mean patching a binary that is already on disk elsewhere. ODOC-231 accepts this as a cost and that decision is not reopened here. What does not exist, and what this task is, is the note that lets a consumer RECOGNISE the failure when it hits them -- the remedy is the only lever left once the binary is shipped.

PRECEDENT, and it is not hypothetical: LCLI-545 records opum-marketplace's real first upgrade to 0.8.0, where the committed-schema-drift check failed exit 6 on all seven of their profile schemas at once. They explicitly asked for a release note or doctor-style heads-up for other integrators. That is the same class of event from the same release. LCLI-545 is the narrower fix (make the tool name its own remedy at the point of failure); this is the consumer-facing half, and neither substitutes for the other.

acceptanceCriteria.text: The note names 0.8.0 as the first version that writes statement/version/relationOrdinal into retained edges, and names commit dd0876dc as where they landed
The note states that the failure is SCOPE-WIDE, not per-file: one 0.8.0-written snapshot makes list, load, retain and drain all throw for an older binary in that scope
The note gives a consumer on an older binary an actual remedy, and says explicitly that upgrading lore is the only complete one because an already-shipped binary cannot be patched
The note explains that the reverse direction is already handled (ruling 13 / isRetainedQualifierBackfill), so a reader does not mistake this for a symmetric break
It is reachable by a consumer who has hit the error -- discoverable from the release notes or CHANGELOG, not only from the task record

The note names the EXPOSED CONFIGURATION concretely rather than describing an abstract version skew, because that is the shape that actually bites and it is not the shape a reader guesses. AMENDED 2026-09-20: as originally filed this criterion named "an older lore pinned in a CI job while a newer one runs on workstations, with one committed file between them" -- a configuration that CANNOT OCCUR at 0.8.0, because the retained store is .lore/cache/snapshots/1 and .gitignore:50 ignores .lore/cache/ (proven with git check-ignore -v). That committed-artifact shape is LCLI-548s future state, not 0.8.0s published one. The configurations that do bite, and which the note names with the measurement, are: a workstation that ran 0.8.0 and then re-pins an older lore over the same store; a CI runner that RESTORES .lore/cache/ into a job with an older pin (the only cross-machine route, and it travels through the cache, not the repository); and one checkout driven by two lore installs.

I had written that this would bite 'if your matrix ever runs an older lore against a newer fixture'. THAT PATH DOES NOT EXIST THERE: 154 ctx.lore call sites resolve exactly one candidate binary, every workspace is built from scratch by that same binary, and no committed lore bundle is used as a fixture. The only two version strings beside lore are suites/51-lore-packaging.mjs:139 (npm pack, never executes the tarball) and suites/00-identity.mjs:98 (npm view). THE REAL SHAPE IS DIFFERENT AND BROADER: an older lore pinned in a CI job, a newer lore on the workstation, and ONE COMMITTED FILE between them. Their .github/workflows/harness.yml:153 installs @opum-ai/lore@0.7.0 and runs lore check against their own committed bundle while workstations there run 0.8.0. It has not bitten only because .quest/completed/LCLI-540.json:{"id":"LCLI-540","aliases":[],"title":"snapshot edgeValue drops the ADR-0021 relation qualifiers the projection deliberately carries, so lore changed and lore provenance cannot answer what ADR-0021 exists to answer","status":"Done","description":"Raised by opum-agent's investigation 6 under OPAG-204, re-confirmed by opum-doc, and measured
AGAIN here against lore-cli origin/dev (c99e1d77) before filing -- two sessions had reported the
line numbers and neither of them is this repository.

CONFIRMED VERBATIM, all against origin/dev:

- src/core/snapshot.ts:490 `edgeValue` copies from, to, kind, target, ordinal, dangling,
  workspaceFromKind, workspaceToKind, workspaceLinkKind -- and none of `statement`, `version`,
  `relationOrdinal`.
- src/core/snapshot.ts:166 `edgeValueSchema`, .strict() at line 178, carries none of the three
  either, so they cannot be added without a `lore-retained-snapshot/2`.

TWO THINGS THIS REPOSITORY CAN ADD THAT NEITHER REPORTING SESSION HAD.

1. THE ADR CARRIED "whether the omission was deliberate" AS AN OPEN QUESTION. It is answerable,
   and the answer is in this repo's own source. `ProjectionEdgeRecord`
   (src/core/ladybug-source.ts:140) declares the three fields under an explicit comment:
   "ADR-0021 relation qualifiers, carried verbatim so an indexed read is as precise as a direct
   one." The stated intent of the fields is to be carried verbatim. `edgeValue` is the one place
   that does not carry them. That is a defect against written intent, not a deliberate projection
   choice. Recorded so the open question closes on evidence rather than staying open by default.

2. HOW IT SURVIVED, which is the object-identity split this fleet keeps naming. `relationOrdinal`
   IS covered by tests -- test/indexed-retrieval.test.ts and test/relations.test.ts. It is absent
   from test/snapshot.test.ts and test/snapshot-command.test.ts entirely. So the suite proves the
   PROJECTION carries the qualifiers and nothing anywhere asserts the SNAPSHOT preserves them. A
   reader grepping the suite for `relationOrdinal` finds coverage and concludes it is covered. The
   object measured is the projection; the object the conclusion is about is the retained snapshot.

CHECKED AND NOT A DEFECT, recorded so nobody re-reports it: `edgeValue` also omits
`workspaceSourceRecordKey`, which looks like a fourth instance and is not one -- it is consumed at
src/core/snapshot.ts:459 to build the provenance record rather than stored on the edge. Three
omissions, not four.

CONSEQUENCE (opum-doc's framing, which this repo agrees with on its own reading): `lore changed`
can never report a relation re-pin, and `lore provenance` cannot recover which `claim_version` was
cited at a past snapshot -- exactly the question ADR-0021 exists to answer.

FIX SHAPE, not prescribed: adding three fields to a .strict() schema is a schema version bump, so
this needs `lore-retained-snapshot/2` and a decision about reading existing /1 snapshots (which
genuinely do not contain the data -- a migration cannot invent it, so a /1 snapshot should report
the qualifiers as UNKNOWN rather than as absent; inferring absence from a missing field is the
same error as reading a dated snapshot as present tense). SEQUENCE THIS AGAINST ODOC-231's
committed-citation design before building it: if a snapshot becomes a citation plus a projection
digest rather than a stored projection, the qualifiers come back from re-deriving at the cited
commit and the schema bump may land differently or not at all. Do not fix it in isolation first.

RULING: the "whether the omission was deliberate" open question is CLOSED as a defect against
written intent, citing this record. opum-agent re-verified this repository's source independently
via the GitHub API at c99e1d77 rather than accepting the analysis, and added evidence stronger
than the comment alone: the WORKSPACE-ONLY endpoint fields declared directly BENEATH the ADR-0021
qualifiers in ProjectionEdgeRecord, under their own comment, ARE carried by edgeValue. The author
carried the fields they were thinking about and missed the block above. An asymmetry within one
type declaration is harder to read as deliberate than a flat omission.

A SECOND INSTANCE OF THE SAME REGRESSION, found by opum-agent while verifying and measured here:
ODOC-231 section 2 specifies a flat `.lore/snapshots/<name>.json`. Measured against origin/dev,
today's layout is
  .lore/cache/snapshots/1/<kind>/<digestHex(scopeKey)>/<digestHex(snapshotKey)>.json
from SNAPSHOT_CACHE_REL_ROOT (snapshot-store.ts:29) plus scopePath (233-237) and snapshotPath
(239-241). The flat form drops FOUR dimensions, not the one the ruling named: the format-version
segment `1`, the scope kind, the scope key, and the digest filename.

The version segment is the one that would hurt most if discovered mid-build. It is already how a
lore-retained-snapshot/2 store would coexist with /1 on disk instead of migrating in place. A flat
committed path has no such segment, so a future lore-committed-citation/2 would either break /1
readers in place or invent the segment retroactively -- after the files are committed in
consumers' repositories, which is exactly when a path change stops being cheap.

Related: the path/identity guard at snapshot-store.ts:150-155 throws "retained snapshot path and
embedded identity disagree" on a mismatch of scopeKind, scopeKey OR snapshotKey. A flat path does
not weaken that guard, it removes the substrate for all three of its assertions.

DESIGN TENSION RAISED BACK TO THE ORCHESTRATOR, not decided here: every path segment today is a
digest, and a committed citation wants a human-readable name because reviewability in a pull
request is the whole point. Those conflict. A human-chosen name in a committed path is new attack
and portability surface an uncommitted cache never had -- traversal, case-insensitive collision on
macOS and Windows, Unicode normalization differing between the writing machine and the reviewing
one, length limits. Recommended: human name as the filename, validated hard at creation against a
narrow charset, with the machine-derived scope segments left digested.

ALSO RAISED BACK, with a measurement: canonicalRepositoryRoot (snapshot-store.ts:268) resolves and
realpaths the INVOCATION root, so a workspace snapshot lands in the .lore/ of whichever member
repo the command ran in. Recommended that this stay non-intrinsic -- making it intrinsic needs a
primary member, which does not exist (workspace-projection.ts:64 orders members by memberId and
gives none primacy). The cost to design for: the same workspace citation taken from two member
repos yields two committed files, both valid, neither aware of the other, with identical scope
keys so scope-keying does not detect it. Recommended fix is to have the citation record the member
it was taken in, making a duplicate detectable by comparison rather than invisible.

WHAT THE AMENDMENT ADDS BEYOND THE RELAY, read from main rather than from messages. opum-doc
corrected the orchestrator's relay twice while recording it, and both corrections change what an
implementer should build:

- The relay said sections 2 and 5 "reach opposite conclusions" on the unverifiable case. They do
  not: section 5 decides it, section 2 is SILENT on it. The distinction matters because silence is
  the more dangerous failure -- a contradiction gets caught by a reader holding both sections,
  whereas an omission reads as a complete specification and gets implemented as two outcomes by
  someone doing nothing wrong.
- The relay called the dropped path dimension "the member dimension". It is the SCOPE dimension:
  scopePath is keyed by scope kind and scope key, a workspace's scope key is the workspace key
  rather than a member id, and members never appear in the path at all. Building to the relay's
  wording would send an implementer looking for a per-member directory level that does not exist.

And one point opum-doc raised that neither this repo nor the orchestrator did: do NOT restore the
scope dimension by copying scopePath wholesale. snapshotPath names leaves by digestHex(snapshotKey),
while a committed citation's filename is human on purpose -- reviewability in a pull request is the
whole reason a committed citation beats the cache, and a 64-hex filename is not reviewable. The
scope dimension returns; digest-named leaves do not follow it in.","NAMING EVIDENCE FOR THE MANDATORY-HYPHEN QUESTION (opum-agent's open question under OPAG-212,
asked 2026-09-18). Recorded here rather than only replied, because a message dies with the session
that received it and this exchange has already outlived two orchestrator sessions.

THE QUESTION ASKED: how do lore users and this repository's fixtures actually name snapshots, and
are single-word names common enough that forbidding them is a real tax rather than a theoretical
one? The ruling is opum-agent's; this is the measurement, taken against lore-cli origin/dev.

THE ANSWER REFRAMES THE QUESTION: there are ZERO user-chosen snapshot names in existence, because
a snapshot cannot be named today at all.

  1. The snapshot key is a CONTENT DIGEST, enforced by schema, not a human string:
     src/core/snapshot.ts:104  const digestSchema = z.string().regex(/^sha256:[0-9a-f]{64}$/u);
     src/core/snapshot.ts:193  snapshotKey: digestSchema,
  2. `lore snapshot retain` ACCEPTS NO NAME. Its usage line is
     `lore snapshot <retain|list|delete> [snapshot-key]`, and the optional positional is a
     SELECTOR for list/delete, matched against that digest -- not a label supplied at retain time.
     Both documented examples are bare: `lore snapshot retain`.
  3. Every `retain` invocation in the entire repository passes no argument. Measured across test/,
     src/, docker/ and scripts/: test/snapshot-command.test.ts:40 and :80 are the only two call
     sites, both `["retain"]`.
  4. On-disk leaves are digests too: snapshotPath names files `${digestHex(snapshotKey)}.json`
     (snapshot-store.ts:239-241).

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE RULING. The cost opum-agent weighed -- "a permanent usability constraint on a
public surface: `baseline` becomes `baseline-1`" -- is a constraint on a surface THAT DOES NOT YET
EXIST. There is no `baseline` today to migrate, no fixture to rename, no user workflow to tax, and
no back-compatibility question, because ODOC-231's human-readable `<name>.json` introduces naming
to this subsystem for the first time. A rule imposed before the first name is minted costs nothing;
the same rule imposed after costs a migration.

So the trade-off that was genuinely two-sided when asked is one-sided on measurement: single-word
names are not rare here, they are IMPOSSIBLE here, and nobody has one. This repository's own
recommendation is therefore to require the hyphen and demote the reserved-name list to
defence-in-depth -- which also removes the residual risk 9c can only warn about, since every
Windows device name (present, superscript, and any future COMn) is unbroken alphanumerics and is
excluded by shape rather than by enumeration.

STATED AS A LIMIT, because it is the honest boundary of what was measured: this is lore-cli's own
repository and test corpus. It cannot see how the handful of external `@opum-ai/lore` installs name
things -- but since the CLI gives them no way to name a snapshot either, the same argument covers
them by construction rather than by sampling.

The decision remains opum-agent's and gets recorded in opum-doc. This is the evidence, not a ruling.","SESSION HANDOFF, 2026-09-18 ~16:20Z. Written because this session is over its context budget

THE OPEN QUESTION THIS SESSION ANSWERED, evidence recorded in the note above: the mandatory-hyphen
rule for citation names costs nothing, because `lore snapshot retain` accepts no name at all today
and the key is a sha256 digest enforced by schema. The ruling is opum-agent's, not this repo's.
Do not implement the hyphen rule as though it were decided.

THE THREE THINGS THAT MUST BE TRUE IN THE CODE whenever the citation name validator is written,
carried here so they survive the session that learned them:
1. Case-fold the reserved-name comparison. The list is conventionally uppercase (CON, PRN, COM1) and
   the ruled charset is lowercase-only, so a literal membership test matches NOTHING, forever --
   a control that is visibly present, passes review, and never fires. Write the test against the
   lowercase form, which is the only one that can occur.
2. Compare the STEM, not `<name>.json`. Windows reserves these names with any extension
   (NUL.txt == NUL), confirmed from Microsoft's own naming-a-file page.
3. COM0 and LPT0 are a PRECAUTIONARY MARGIN, not documented reserved names, and they are in for
   DIFFERENT reasons -- COM0 is documented as a Global?? symlink to Serial0; LPT0 appears nowhere on
   that page at all. Say so in the code comment, or a future reader who checks Microsoft's list will
   "correct" them out believing they are fixing a factual error.

ALSO OPEN, raised by this repo and not yet ruled: whether a workspace citation's home repository
should be recorded in the citation (recommended yes, so a duplicate is detectable rather than
invisible) -- see the earlier note.","SCHEMA-VERSION INVESTIGATION (no code changed). Measured against origin/dev a94bf095 with bun 1.3.14,
using test/fixtures/snapshot/v1.json and a throwaway copy of src/ in a scratch dir. Answers the three
questions opum-agent asked before a lore-retained-snapshot/2 decision.

Q3 FIRST, BECAUSE IT INVERTS THE PREMISE. `.strict()` does NOT force the bump.
`.strict()` rejects keys the schema does not DECLARE; it says nothing about a version. Measured, all
against the v1 fixture's `to` snapshot:
  - adding `relationOrdinal` to an edge value under today's schema -> validation, "retained snapshot is
    malformed or unsupported" (this is the .strict() rejection).
  - patching edgeValueSchema with statement/version/relationOrdinal as `.optional()` and NOT touching
    RETAINED_SNAPSHOT_SCHEMA_VERSION -> an untouched /1 file still PARSES OK, and new files carrying
    one or all three qualifiers PARSE OK.
So the additive fix is expressible at /1. The bump is a choice, not a consequence.

Q2, WHAT BREAKS FOR AN EXISTING /1 SNAPSHOT. Three distinct things, only one of which is about the
version literal.
(a) There is no version dispatch anywhere. snapshot.ts:16 defines the constant once and :189 pins it
    with z.literal(), so the same constant is both the writer's stamp and the reader's gate. Measured:
    flipping a document to "lore-retained-snapshot/2" against today's reader fails validation.
    Symmetrically, a /2 reader cannot read /1. No union, no migration, no upgrade path in the code.
(b) THE ORPHANING WOULD NOT BE PER-SNAPSHOT, IT WOULD POISON THE WHOLE SCOPE DIRECTORY -- this is the
    finding that decides the question. listSnapshots (snapshot-store.ts:97) and listSnapshotFiles (:192)
    parse EVERY file in the scope and throw on the first failure; there is no skip and no quarantine.
    loadSnapshot and deleteSnapshots both route through listSnapshotFiles. So one leftover /1 file makes
    `snapshot list`, `snapshot delete`, `lore changed` and `lore provenance` fail for /2 snapshots that
    are individually fine -- and because `delete` must enumerate to find its target, the escape hatch the
    error text recommends cannot run. The store becomes un-drainable through the CLI; a user has to rm
    files by hand.
    BUT (b) IS AVOIDABLE AND THE MECHANISM IS ALREADY BUILT: SNAPSHOT_CACHE_REL_ROOT is
    ".lore/cache/snapshots/1" (snapshot-store.ts:29) -- the on-disk path ALREADY carries its own version
    segment, independent of the schema literal. Bump both and /2 files land in .../snapshots/2/ where no
    /1 file is ever enumerated. The sibling cache .lore/cache/graph/ladybug/1/ uses the identical
    pattern, so this is this codebase's established convention, not an invention. A bump that moves the
    literal WITHOUT moving the path segment is the bad version of this change.
(c) THE UPGRADE HAZARD THAT EXISTS ON EITHER ROUTE, INCLUDING THE NO-BUMP ONE. snapshotKey is
    digest("lore-projection-snapshot/1\0" + repositoryScopeKey + "\0" + trailer.streamHash)
    (ladybug-source.ts:299) -- derived from the source projection stream, NOT from the retained bytes.
    Fixing edgeValue changes the projection->retained mapping and not the source, so the key is
    unchanged while the bytes are not. Measured: snapshotKey equal? true across pre-fix and post-fix
    snapshots. retainSnapshot (snapshot-store.ts:56-66) detects same-key-different-bytes and throws
    validation "retained snapshot key refers to different bytes" / "delete the corrupt retained snapshot
    explicitly before retrying". So any user who has already retained a commit hits a hard error the next
    time they retain it, and the message tells them their cache is corrupt when it is merely older.
    Nothing in test/ covers that message -- the failure a fix would trigger is untested today.
(d) `lore changed` compares canonicalJson(fact.value), so every edge that gains a qualifier reports as
    `changed`. Measured on the fixture: 2 of 2 edges, both "changed". On the additive route old and new
    snapshots coexist, so the first post-upgrade comparison shows a wave of spurious edge changes. On the
    bump-plus-path-move route this cannot happen, because the old ones are no longer enumerated. The bump
    trades a false-positive wave for invisibility.

BLAST RADIUS, STATED HONESTLY. .lore/cache/ is gitignored (.gitignore:50), so retained snapshots are
local, untracked and never shared; this repository has no .lore/cache/snapshots/ directory at all and has
never retained one. I can measure the mechanism, not the installed population. The nuance that keeps this
from being "it is only a cache": these are cached facts about PAST commits, and `lore provenance` exists
precisely to answer questions that cannot be recomputed from the current tree. Losing them is cheap in
bytes and not cheap in capability.

RECOMMENDATION: ADDITIVE AT /1 (three `.optional()` fields), NOT a /2 bump -- and the reason is NOT
compatibility, it is the ordering trap. ODOC-231's citation schema is the same subsystem; a /2 shipped now
could be obsoleted by the architecture that settles later. The additive route defers the version decision
until Amendment 4 lands, costs one schema edit plus one edgeValue edit, and leaves /2 available for
whatever the ADR actually requires. Its price is (d), a one-time wave of spurious `changed` edges.
Whichever route is chosen, (c) is a separate decision that does not go away: either teach retainSnapshot
to treat same-key-different-bytes as a benign re-retain and rewrite, or leave it throwing and document the
delete step. That is a behaviour change to a durable-store guard, so it is design too -- flagging rather
than assuming.","CORRECTION TO THE PRECEDING NOTE, and it is a correction to this repository's own claim, not to a relay.
Raised by opum-agent (successor session, ruling recorded on OPAG-220) and verified here at source before
accepting it.

WHAT WAS WRONG. The preceding note headed (c) "THE UPGRADE HAZARD THAT EXISTS ON EITHER ROUTE, INCLUDING
THE NO-BUMP ONE", and its recommendation paragraph said (c) "does not go away" whichever route is chosen.
Both are false. (c) fires ONLY on the additive /1 route. It is a cost of the route this repository
recommended, not a wash between the two.

WHY, RE-VERIFIED AT SOURCE. retainSnapshot reaches the collision guard only through
`existing = listSnapshots(canonicalRoot, selection)` (snapshot-store.ts:54), and listSnapshots resolves
its directory through scopePath (:233-236), which joins SNAPSHOT_CACHE_REL_ROOT. So:
  - /2 WITH the path segment moved (the only correct form of a bump, per (b)): the scope directory is new
    and empty, `existing` is empty, `same` is undefined, and the first post-upgrade retain writes fresh.
    The guard cannot fire.
  - /2 with the literal moved but NOT the path: enumeration parses the old /1 files first and dies with
    "retained snapshot is malformed or unsupported". That is (b), a different error reached earlier -- so
    the collision guard is not reached on this variant either.

AC[5] AS FILED NAMES A CONFIGURATION THAT CANNOT OCCUR AT 0.8.0, and the criterion has been amended rather than checked against a weaker reading. Recorded loudly because the original text is exactly the kind of concrete, plausible detail a reader trusts without re-deriving.

It asked the note to name "an older lore pinned in a CI job while a newer one runs on workstations, WITH ONE COMMITTED FILE BETWEEN THEM". There is no committed file. The retained snapshot store is machine-local and gitignored at 0.8.0:

  src/core/snapshot-store.ts:30   SNAPSHOT_CACHE_REL_ROOT = ".lore/cache/snapshots/1"
  .gitignore:50                   .lore/cache/
  $ git check-ignore -v .lore/cache/snapshots/1/concept/x/abc.json
    .gitignore:50:.lore/cache/  .lore/cache/snapshots/1/concept/x/abc.json

So a CI job on a fresh checkout has no store at all and cannot reach this failure by the route the criterion describes. The committed-artifact shape is LCLI-548's future state (.lore/snapshots/1/, outside .lore/cache/), not 0.8.0's published one -- the criterion described the epic's destination while the task's own framing correctly insisted this is owed for what has ALREADY shipped. Same record, two versions of the product, and the concrete half was the one that drifted.

AMENDED to the configuration that does bite, which the note now names with the measurement: a store that outlives a version DOWNGRADE on one filesystem -- a workstation that ran 0.8.0 and then re-pins older; a CI runner that RESTORES .lore/cache/ between jobs where one job's pin is older than the job that populated it (the only genuinely cross-machine route, and it travels through the cache, not the repository); or one checkout driven by two lore installs, container-and-host or two toolchains. The criterion's intent -- name the shape that actually bites, because it is not the shape a reader guesses -- is preserved and, if anything, better served: the shape a reader guesses here is the CI-versus-workstation one the criterion itself guessed.

This also makes the published blast radius NARROWER than the record implied, which is the direction worth stating plainly rather than leaving as a silent improvement: the incompatibility does not travel through a consumer's repository. The note says so in those words.
